extraction.name: CT-RATE
extraction.description: CT-RATE is a public dataset that pairs 3D medical images with corresponding textual reports. CT-RATE comprises 25,692 non-contrast 3D chest CT scans from 21,304 unique patients. Each scan is accompanied by its corresponding radiology report. The dataset includes 50,188 reconstructed 3D chest CT volumes (over 14.3 million 2D slices) from 25,692 scans of 21,304 patients with corresponding radiology reports. Each volume is annotated with 18 abnormalities, supporting extensive validation and fine-tuning. CT-RATE is fully open-source. The dataset is curated from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital and includes non-contrast chest CT volumes acquired between May 2015 and January 2023. The patients range in age from 18 to 102 years, with a mean of 48.8 years and a mode of 40 years. The sex distribution is 41.6% female and 58.4% male. 61.5% of the scans are taken using Philips CT scanners, 30.1% with Siemens scanners, and 8.4% with PNMS (Philips-Neusoft Medical Systems) scanners. The CT volumes are provided in various resolutions: 65.4% in 512x512 px, 4.2% in 768x768 px, and 30.4% in 1024x1024 px. The pixel spacing in the axial (XY) plane ranges from 0.227 to 1.416 mm, with a mean of 0.605 mm, while slice thickness ranges from 0.035 to 6 mm, with a mean of 1.231 mm. The number of slices per volume ranges from 100 to 600, averaging 304.7 with a mode of 255 slices. The radiology reports are structured into four sections: clinical information, technique, findings, and impression. The dataset also includes organ-level anatomical segmentation labels generated using a state-of-the-art segmentation model.

extraction.rai:dataCollection: The CT-RATE dataset was curated from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital. It consists of non-contrast chest CT volumes and corresponding radiology text reports. Data was acquired between May 2015 and January 2023. The dataset includes 50,188 reconstructed CT volumes from 25,692 distinct CT experiments conducted on 21,304 unique patients. Every reconstructed volume from the hospital database was incorporated to facilitate a thorough evaluation of various abnormalities. The cohort was divided into two groups: 20,000 patients for training and 1,304 for validation. To uphold patient privacy, all chest CT volumes, associated metadata, and radiology text reports were anonymized. This involved removing personal information using regular expressions for date-related information and patient-doctor identifiers. Anonymized reports were translated from Turkish to English using the Google Translate API, and bilingual final-year medical students reviewed and corrected all translations, ensuring coherence and removal of residual personal information. Only English versions are included. Quality control measures for CT volumes included excluding volumes with contrast material or body parts other than the chest. Each chest CT volume’s orientation was standardized by examining its metadata, and all identifying information was removed from the metadata. Organ-level anatomical segmentation labels were generated using a state-of-the-art segmentation model [51].
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Physical data collection, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Chest CT volumes and corresponding radiology text reports from Istanbul Medipol University Mega Hospital.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Our preprocessing approach, inspired by previous work [20], involved several key steps to standardize all chest CT volumes in the dataset. First, each volume was resized to achieve uniform spacing of 0.75 mm in the x-axis and y-axis and 1.5 mm in the z-axis. The CT volumes were then either center-cropped or padded to reach a consistent resolution of 480x480x240, ensuring comprehensive inclusion of the patient’s relevant area for the interpretation. Subsequently, we converted each CT volume to Hounsfield Unit (HU) values using intercept and slope values from the metadata. HU values, a measure of radiodensity, were clipped to a range of -1000 to 1000. During training, these values were normalized to a range of -1 to 1. The CT-RATE dataset contains the original raw data and all preprocessing scripts are provided in our GitHub repository.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: To develop an automated label extractor model, 1,000 reports were manually annotated by merging findings and impression sections, as some abnormalities are not explicitly mentioned in a single section. This created a multi-label dataset for each report, identifying 18 abnormalities. Conditions not referenced in either section were considered absent. Similar conditions were grouped: left and right mucoid impactions under mucoid impaction, and various lung opacities (lung opacity, density increase, and ground-glass opacities) under lung opacity. Lung and fissural nodules were categorized as lung nodules. The annotated reports were divided into training (80%, 800 reports) and validation (20%, 200 reports) sets. Leveraging this dataset, the RadBERT-RoBERTa-4m model [34] was finetuned and then applied to classify the remaining 24,692 reports. These classified reports serve three purposes: training the supervised baseline model, finetuning CT-CLIP, and internal evaluation of the models.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Bilingual final-year medical students reviewed and corrected all translations of anonymized reports.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Patient age, sex, and medical history (clinical information section of radiology reports). All personal information was anonymized to uphold patient privacy.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The open-source release of CT-RATE, CT-CLIP, and CT-CHAT not only addresses critical challenges in 3D medical imaging but also lays the groundwork for future innovations in medical AI and improved patient care. The models have the potential to address the challenge of manual report generation from complex images, which is time-consuming and prone to errors, by efficiently identifying pathologies, reducing the workload on radiologists, and potentially saving lives in situations where immediate radiological expertise is not available. The user-friendly graphical interface makes CT-CHAT a valuable tool for educational and clinical research settings and invites a wider audience to engage with and contribute to the evolution of interactive AI-driven inference in clinical practice.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Biases inherent to our single-institution dataset may influence our self-supervised training. Although we curate a large and diverse set of volume-report pairs, the data originates from a single geographic and clinical setting, which may limit the generalizability of our models to other populations. An ablation study revealed that performance increases with larger training sets, suggesting that incorporating data from multiple institutions and more diverse patient populations could further enhance model robustness.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: 1. Biases inherent to our single-institution dataset may influence self-supervised training, limiting generalizability to other populations. Performance increases with larger training sets, suggesting the need for data from multiple institutions and diverse patient populations. 2. CT-CLIP depends on the specific terminology used in reports and the choice of prompts during zero-shot detection. Variability in disease descriptions across radiology reports can affect detection accuracy. Prompt engineering experiments were conducted, and the best-performing prompt was selected, but continued optimization may further improve performance. 3. Evaluation of CT-CHAT faces limitations due to the lack of pretrained 3D medical multimodal AI assistants for benchmarking. Comparisons were made against 2D models using Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs (DRRs) to represent 3D information, but the absence of true 3D benchmarks highlights the need for further development and validation of multimodal AI assistants in 3D medical imaging. 4. The quality of CT-CHAT's generated reports remains insufficient for clinical use, despite outperforming other models. 5. Current models are limited to chest CT volumes. Future work should extend CT-RATE, CT-CLIP, and CT-CHAT to include other 3D imaging modalities (MRI, PET) and anatomical regions to broaden clinical applicability.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation, Fine Tuning. The dataset is used for developing CT-CLIP, a CT-focused contrastive language-image pretraining framework designed for broad applications without the need for task-specific training. CT-CLIP can be used in multi-abnormality detection and case retrieval. The dataset is also used to fine-tune CT-CHAT, a vision-language foundational chat model for 3D chest CT volumes, on over 2.7 million question-answer pairs. The dataset is also used for benchmarking against state-of-the-art models.
